segments.text: Sonae. The agent team that stands watch over your family. Built for the AWS Agents for Humans hackathon, on the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

Japan asks every household to prepare a personal evacuation timeline: who does what, at which official alert level. That means reading the municipal hazard map for your own address, learning which evacuation site is designated for which disaster, because they are not the same site, and negotiating it all with your family. It is homework assigned to every household in a country of a hundred and twenty three million people. It is the kind of homework that waits until the river is rising.

And the people with the least capacity to do it are the ones who die. In Japan's recent flood disasters, most of the dead were elderly: about sixty five percent in the twenty nineteen typhoon this demo replays, about eighty percent in the floods of twenty twenty. Often an aging parent, alone in the family home, hours away from their children.

The night of Typhoon Hagibis, twenty nineteen. At three thirty in the afternoon, the first emergency heavy rain warning ever issued for Nagano Prefecture, while it was still light. The emergency evacuation order for the riverside districts came at twenty three forty, in darkness and driving rain. After one in the morning the river came over the bank at Hoyasu, and the district flooded to the rooftops. The information was public the whole time. What families lacked was an agent on watch.

This is Sonae. Give it one address, and a few sentences about your family. A Cartographer agent reads the statutory hazard maps at that address. A Planner drafts the family's timeline, tuned to a grandmother's knees. And before anything reaches you, an adversarial Verifier re-derives every claim from the same official data. You review the plan, and approve it. Once, calmly. From here, Sonae is authorized to act.
Now, October eleventh, twenty nineteen, replayed minute by minute from the official record. The day before landfall: level one. Charge the phone. Pack the medication. While the sky is clear.
Saturday afternoon, the river reaches advisory levels. Level two. Valuables upstairs, walking shoes by the door.

Three thirty PM. An emergency heavy rain warning, the first ever issued for Nagano Prefecture. Formally, that is a level five equivalent signal for rainfall. But level five tells you to protect yourself where you are, and the national guidance is to finish evacuating while you still can. So Sonae applies a rule that is written into the plan, into the repository, and into the journal: it pushes the plan's level four step. Complete the evacuation now. And watch the verifier. It rejected the first draft, because the subject line claimed an evacuation order that did not exist yet, then approved the corrected message. Sunset is at seventeen sixteen. There is still light to walk in.

Then, discipline. Landslide advisories for other districts. River bulletins the plan already covers. The Sentinel stands by through all of them. A family that trusts its agent is a family that acts when it speaks.

Eight fifty PM. Bulletin number seven: upstream at Shinonoi-Yokota, the river came over its left bank around twenty past eight, and the city has declared level five. Final confirmation that everyone is out, and that nobody goes back in. Safety check-ins open on every phone.

Twenty three forty. The city escalates to an emergency evacuation order. This is the moment the real residents of Hoyasu were told to leave. At eight minutes past one, the river came over the bank at their doorstep; the breach was announced at six in the morning. Sonae's verified push had gone out eight hours and nine minutes before that order. On the plan's own two hour walking allowance, Yoshiko is at the shelter before six in the evening.

After the water, Japanese neighborhoods confirm safety with paper name lists, carried door to door. Sonae's circle mode replaces the paper, not the neighbors. Live check-ins across households, and a Coordinator agent that tells the chairman exactly which door to knock on first: the eighty eight year old, still unconfirmed.

None of this is a demo trick. Every line on this slide is quoted from the journal committed in the repository. AI prose fails closed: unverified text is never sent. The official signal fails open: relayed verbatim rather than silenced. And the family's approval is the authorization boundary. Sonae maps official signals onto the plan they signed. It never originates an evacuation judgment of its own.

Under the hood, a self-correcting Strands graph builds the plan, and a verified pipeline runs the watch, with typed JSON between agents and flight recorder hooks on every tool call. It runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: deployed, with per household state synchronized to S3, and an EventBridge heartbeat. We verified the whole chain in the cloud, including the planning graph converging inside the runtime. On a calm day, a watch cycle costs zero model tokens. Boring is the job.

Everything you saw runs on public government data. Hazard maps, shelter registries, live weather feeds. Built for Japan, and portable to any country that publishes its hazards. Sonae. Because the next Hagibis is already forming, and every family deserves someone on watch.
